rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

human.problem: Several self-deprecating jokes put Papa Dorin in modern human situations outside his bakery. In Stop 1 card 10, he keeps his phone on a nightstand and fights the snooze button. In Stop 1 card 15, he builds a shelf and ends up with extra screws. In Stop 2 card 12, he tangles a phone charger. papa-dorin.md lets him use everyday adult life for comparisons and lets his jokes make up small moments "around his bakery." It also says he never adds anything new to his world. It doesn't say whether he can claim personal habits like owning a phone or furniture.
human.question: Can Papa Dorin tell first-person jokes where he owns or uses everyday modern things like a phone, a nightstand or flat-pack furniture? Or should everyday-life comparisons be about people in general ("That's like someone who..."), with his own self-deprecating jokes kept to the bakery, the drawer and the Dorinverse?

human.problem: Several jokes give Papa Dorin personal modern belongings and habits in the Dorinverse: a phone and a snooze button on his nightstand (stop 1 card 10), and a phone charger he tangled himself (stop 2 card 11). papa-dorin.md lets him use everyday adult life for comparisons, and lets his jokes make up small moments and habits around his bakery. It also says he never adds anything new to his own world. It doesn't say whether he can claim to own and use modern items like these himself.
human.question: In his self-deprecating jokes, can Papa Dorin say he personally owns and uses modern items like a phone, snooze alarm, nightstand or phone charger? Or must everyday-life comparisons stay general, like 'that's like hitting snooze,' without placing those items in his own life?
